lead: A body with mass resists being spun up. The resistance is not just the mass; it also depends on how far each bit of mass lies from the axis. Mass moment of inertia turns that idea into one integral, I = ∫ r² dm, with dm in kg, r in m and I in kg·m². It lets you compare a solid disc, a ring and a flywheel, and it appears wherever a machine part must be accelerated in rotation: vehicle wheels, pump shafts, motors, and the blades of a fan.
prereq: You need: second moment of area for the element idea, parallel axis theorem for shifting, and radius of gyration for I = m k².

sections.h3: The integral and the radius of gyration

blocks.text: In second moment of area, each area element was multiplied by the square of its distance from an axis. For a real body, replace area by mass. A kilogram near the axis is easy to spin; the same kilogram at the rim of a wheel is much harder. The mass moment of inertia measures that difference.

Take an element of mass dm at perpendicular distance r from the chosen axis. Then I = ∫ r² dm. Here dm is in kg, r is in m, and I is in kg·m². For a uniform body of density ρ in kg/m³, dm = ρ dV, and the total mass is m = ρV. The element volume dV must be in m³.
I = ∫ r² dm = ρ ∫ r² dV
blocks.where: I is the mass moment of inertia about the axis (kg·m²); r is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the element (m); dm is the element mass (kg); ρ is density (kg/m³); dV is the element volume (m³).

blocks.text: The same body has different I about different axes. A centroidal axis passes through the centre of mass. For a parallel axis a distance d away, I = Ī + m d², where Ī is the centroidal value, m is the total mass in kg and d is in m. This is the parallel axis theorem with mass in place of area.

Write I = m k², where k is the radius of gyration in m and m is in kg. Then k = √(I/m). It is the single distance at which the whole mass could be placed to give the same I. It is not necessarily equal to the outer radius of the body.

sections.h3: Standard results for plates and solids

blocks.text: The table gives results for the axis named. Check the axis before using a formula. If the required axis is parallel but not the same, shift the tabulated centroidal value with m d².

Thin rectangular plate, axis along an edge of length a
Rectangular prism, sides a, b, c, centroidal axis parallel to side c
Solid cylinder, radius r, height h, central axis
Solid cone, base radius r, central axis
Solid sphere, radius r, any diameter

blocks.text: For the thin plate, a and b are the side lengths in m. The normal axis is perpendicular to the plate through its centroid. The edge formula uses the side of length a as the edge axis and b as the perpendicular width. For the prism, the centroidal axis is parallel to side c; permute the letters for the other two directions.

For the cylinder, r is the radius and h is the height. The transverse centroidal axis is perpendicular to the cylinder axis and passes through the centre of mass. For the cone and sphere, r is the base or sphere radius. A thin ring has all its mass at radius r, so its value is simply m r² about the central normal axis.
Work in metres and kilograms before substituting. A radius of 200 mm is 0.200 m, and 200² is not 0.200².
A composite body is split into standard parts. Holes are parts with negative mass. The total I is the sum of the parts about one chosen axis.

items: Choose the axis for the whole body and draw it.
For each part, find its mass m_i and the perpendicular distance d_i from the chosen axis to its own centroidal axis parallel to it.
Take the centroidal value Ī_i from the table and shift it: I_i = Ī_i + m_i d_i².
Add all I_i. Subtract the contribution of a hole.
Check units in kg·m² and find k = √(I/m).

blocks.text: A flywheel works this way. The rim has most of its mass far from the axis, so it adds a large m d² and gives a large I for a modest total mass. A solid hub near the axis adds little. That is why a ring of the same mass and radius at the same angular speed can store more rotational energy than a solid disc. How I is used in rotation appears in Unit 6.

spec.title: Mass moment of inertia, one rule
spec.aria: A flow builds the mass moment of inertia from the integral of r squared dm and lists the standard values for a plate, a cylinder, a cone and a sphere before combining them.

examples.question: A solid steel disc has radius 200 mm, thickness 50 mm and density 7850 kg/m³. Find its mass, its mass moment of inertia about the central axis, its mass moment of inertia about a diameter through the centre, and its radius of gyration about the central axis. Use metres and kilograms.
steps: Convert to metres: r = 0.200 m and h = 0.050 m.
About the central axis, use I = ½ m r² = 0.5 × 49.323 × (0.200)² = 0.986 kg·m².
About a diameter, use I = m(3r² + h²)/12. Here 3r² = 0.1200 m², h² = 0.0025 m², and their sum is 0.1225 m². Then I = 49.323 × 0.1225 / 12 = 6.042 / 12 = 0.504 kg·m².
Radius of gyration about the central axis: k = √(I/m) = √(0.986 / 49.323) = 0.141 m.
examples.answer: The mass is 49.323 kg, the moment about the central axis is 0.986 kg·m², about a diameter is 0.504 kg·m², and the radius of gyration about the central axis is 0.141 m.
examples.check:
import math
r = 0.200
h = 0.050
rho = 7850
V = math.pi * r**2 * h
m = rho * V
I_axis = 0.5 * m * r**2
I_diam = m * (3*r**2 + h**2) / 12
k = math.sqrt(I_axis / m)
print(round(m, 3))
print(round(I_axis, 3))
print(round(I_diam, 3))
print(round(k, 3))

traps: Using millimetres for r while the mass is in kilograms. The answer becomes 10⁶ times too large. Convert every length to metres first.
Shifting with area A d² from Unit 4 instead of mass m d². The parallel axis rule for mass uses the body's mass.
Using ½ m r² for a thin ring. That value belongs to a solid cylinder; a thin ring about its central normal axis is m r².
Quoting a formula without naming the axis. A cylinder has ½ m r² about its axis but a different value about a transverse centroidal axis.
Putting volume in mm³ with density in kg/m³. The mass comes out a billion times too large. Use m³.

quiz.q: State the mass moment of inertia integral and the unit of each symbol.
quiz.a: I = ∫ r² dm, where dm is element mass in kg, r is perpendicular distance in m, and I is in kg·m².

quiz.q: Why does a thin ring have larger I than a solid disc of the same mass and radius about the central normal axis?
quiz.a: In the ring all mass sits at radius r, so I = m r². In the solid disc much mass lies closer to the axis, giving I = ½ m r².

quiz.q: A thin plate has mass 6 kg, sides 0.4 m and 0.3 m. Find I about the normal centroidal axis and about the edge parallel to the 0.4 m side.
quiz.a: Normal centroidal: I = m(a² + b²)/12 = 6(0.16 + 0.09)/12 = 0.125 kg·m². Edge parallel to the 0.4 m side: I = m b²/3 = 6(0.3²)/3 = 0.180 kg·m², where b = 0.3 m is the perpendicular width.

quiz.q: A composite body is a cylinder plus a thin ring. What must you check before adding tabulated values directly?
quiz.a: Check that every tabulated value is about an axis parallel to the chosen axis, use the centroidal value for each part, find each mass, and shift each part by m d² before adding. Holes are subtracted.

quiz.q: A solid sphere has mass 10 kg and radius 0.2 m. Find I about a diameter.
What does the radius of gyration tell, and what does it not tell?
quiz.a: It gives the distance k where the whole mass could be placed to give the same I, since I = m k². It is not generally the actual outer radius, and it is not a physical point on the body.

beyond: Not for the exam. In machine design, the mass moment of inertia sets the torque needed to accelerate a shaft, a gear or a wheel. Flywheel energy storage uses a heavy rim with large I to store energy as ½ I ω². Robot arms and satellite attitude control need the full inertia tensor, not one number, because the body can spin about three axes. Search for flywheel energy storage, inertia tensor, and rotational dynamics of rigid bodies.
